items.title: Why everyone should be doing therapy
items.summary: I would bet my house that you’re living with something. There is some sickness, pain, or condition you’ve learned to deal with. Because there is no such thing as “perfect” health. Everyone you talk to, everyone you see on the street, everyone in the line at the coffee shop, has something they have to adapt to. It might be something mild, like dry skin in the winter or being nearsighted. It might be a chronically bad back or intermittent migraines. Or, it might be something that requires more of us: diabetes tests, dialysis, the latest cancer treatment. Everyone, everywhere, is dealing with something. Mental health is no different. I’m sometimes asked if I’m an anxious or obsessive person, and my reply is almost always the same. Yes, I can certainly feel anxious, and yes, I can display obsessive behaviors, but am I anxious or obsessive? I don’t think so. I am the way I am, and I have learned how to live with that. We all grow to deal with the world as best we can. I have strategies, tools, and ways of thinking that allow me to operate in the world, and I’m sure you do as well. The question, then, is what tools we can call upon. The French philosopher Georges Canguilhem once argued that we shouldn’t necessarily define “health” as perfect function or as a “no boxes checked” on a health questionnaire. Instead, we should define health in terms of a “margin of tolerance” to the world’s misfortunes. To be healthy is to have hard times, experience pain, and endure mental distress, but to get back up again and to get back to living. “Health” doesn’t mean having nothing wrong with you — it’s when you have the power to live with your something. As any good therapist will tell you, therapy is not limited to the hour you are in the room. It’s a method. It’s a way of thinking. This is a new, members-only newsletter all about how to live well. It’s about the strategies that can help us cure or endure what makes us anxious, lost, or unhappy. It’s about the tools and habits that we can call upon to enjoy the richness of life all the more. This newsletter is about how to be healthy in mind and happy in soul. The first edition — coming this Sunday — will be free to all, and after that, it will be bundled into our membership package , where you can get all of our newsletters, articles, and videos. There, you can also register to join online events with the likes of Carlo Rovelli, Alex O’Connor, and Brené Brown. And, of course, US customers can get our quarterly print magazine for free. Why “The Sunday Epicurean”? Over 2,000 years ago in Athens, a man living with his own “something” started a school. Epicurus had a great bushy beard and a lifetime of digestive issues, and he founded “The Garden” — one of the four big schools of antiquity. In The Garden, students weren’t bothered with abstract mathematics or metaphysics. They spent their days talking about human suffering and human happiness. Their curriculum focused on the natural sciences and what we now call psychology. The Friends of Epicurus, as they were called, were encouraged to have regular, introspective therapy sessions. They’d eat together, walk together, and philosophize together. Because, as Epicurus put it, in the same way that medicine is pointless if it does not cure the diseases of the body, there is no point in philosophy if it does not cure the suffering of the mind. I strongly believe that everyone should be doing therapy. But I define “therapy” in a looser, wider sense. On the one hand, we live in an age of therapy. More and more people go to see psychotherapists and psychiatrists. We’re all much more willing to speak in the language of therapy, and many of us are better at reflecting on our inner lives. As a philosopher and an empirically minded sort, I think these are good trends. Therapy works for a lot of people. But, as any good therapist will tell you, therapy is not limited to the hour you are in the room. It’s a method. It’s a way of thinking. It’s a reorientation of your life that allows you to live better. Limiting “therapy” to once a week leaves us poorer. Medicalizing therapy — pathologizing it — makes it forever curative and reactive. Good therapy is what we keep with us. When Epicureans talk about therapy, they mean it in a broader, lived sense. It’s something we do every day. It’s something we do with all of our friends as much as possible and not just with Dr. Carver at 3 p.m. on Tuesdays. In The Garden, Epicurus told his students to introspect often, to take control of their decisions, and to nurture their relationships. He said we should commit to who we are, what we enjoy, and where we are right now. I think he’s right. It’s why I’ve written an entire book about it, called The Art of Enough . So, The Sunday Epicurean is a kind of philosophical therapy. It’s a weekly heart-to-heart conversation where we explore — together — what might be causing us pain and how we might alleviate it. It’s a sit-down meal with Friends in The Garden where we learn about the ins and outs of human psychology and how we can all enjoy more of life. The Sunday Epicurean is a newsletter about how to avoid pain and find pleasure. These newsletters will give a little of me and invite a little from you. I hope you can join our Garden community. I hope you can share strategies, habits, and insights as much as I can. Because, as the Friends themselves knew, we are all in this together. We all suffer, and we all laugh. We all get lonely, and we all love. We all have to work out how to live with our “something.” So let’s work out how to live well, together. This is an edition of The Sunday Epicurean , a weekly, members-only newsletter from Mini Philosophy. This article Why everyone should be doing therapy is featured on Big Think .

items.title: Let’s Not Make Reading a Wellness Trend
items.summary: A few weeks ago, I settled down on my couch to read Edith Wharton’s novel The House of Mirth on my iPhone. Or actually to reread—my friends had selected this old favorite of mine as a book-club pick, and our meeting was approaching. I was behind; life had gotten in the way of reading. I thought that I might just poke around for a few minutes to remind myself of the plot, but I was struck by the descriptions of the protagonist, Lily Bart, in the opening chapter—her strange combination of artifice and impulsivity. I had forgotten, or never registered, the moment when she says out loud that she would rather be happy than good. I put my phone down, did some things, and picked it up again to read. I lost track of time. But I didn’t really, because I was tracking myself using an app called Readwise Books. In that 40-minute “session,” I read roughly 136 words a minute. My “progress” was +2.1 percent of the novel as a whole. I was trying out “the Strava of reading,” as Readwise’s founders have described their creation—a reference to the popular running app that tracks speed, distance, heart rate, and other stats. These were my results. I n a n essay announcing the app last month , Readwise’s co-founders, Daniel Doyon and Tristan Homsi, ticked off a dizzying array of wellness fads and gadgets that have captured the public imagination in recent years: “Resistance training. Meditation. Cold plunges. Sauna (Finnish and infrared). Sleep tracking. Zone 2 cardio. VO2 max. Recovery. Ten thousand steps a day. Closing your rings. Standing not sitting. Continuous glucose monitors. Light exposure. Light blocking.” Doyon and Homsi posited that another practice should be included on the list, one backed by scientific evidence and known to increase well-being: “Reading books, of course.” They joined a growing chorus of people making the case that reading should be a wellness trend, a form of fitness for the mind—a sales pitch that struck me as new, and a little strange. [ From the August 2026 issue: The end of reading is here ] Reading has long been considered a form of both moral and intellectual self-improvement. See, for instance, James Boswell’s The Life of Samuel Johnson , from 1791: “A young man should read five hours in a day, and so may acquire a great deal of knowledge.” More recently, figures including Oprah Winfrey have espoused reading’s benefits, among them “the way your mind is expanded when you’re exposed to new adventures and ideas.” And in the era of smartphones, many people have advocated for reading as an antidote to fraying attention spans. “Perhaps consuming a few dozen book pages a day should become the new 10,000 daily steps—a basic foundation of activity to maintain cognitive fitness,” the academic Cal Newport wrote earlier this year. This argument about reading and attention has an intuitive logic: Anyone who’s ever stopped scrolling and picked up a book can attest to the soothing, sharpening power of words on a page. But lately, these ideas have progressed into a case for reading’s value that sounds a lot like the way we talk about physical health. Some influencers are promoting reading alongside advice to eat whole foods and lift weights . The 75 Hard Challenge, a program that prescribes two 45-minute daily workouts, also tells participants to read 10 pages of a nonfiction book every day. Jon Finkel’s Books & Biceps newsletter explicitly marries the two. This month, Arnold Schwarzenegger’s weightlifting-focused newsletter included a plug for books, citing a study that showed readers of books had lower risk of mortality than those who didn’t read: “We can’t say that picking up a book will add years to your life. But it’s a low-risk behavior (really, there’s no risk in reading more) with high potential reward.” The point is no longer simply that reading is good for you in an amorphous, holistic sense; it’s that reading might increase your lifespan. This message is well suited for the age of ChatGPT. If going to the gym came into vogue after most American jobs moved away from manual labor, perhaps reading will do the same as more people offload cognitive work to generative AI. “People are coming to the realization that AI is doing more and more of the hard thinking that I used to do at work ,” Doyon told me. “ And my brain is starting to atrophy the same way my body atrophies by sitting in a chair .” And if reading really is the new Zone 2 cardio, it follows that you need a tracker for it, one that allows you to go beyond the traditional Goodreads metric of books per calendar year. In addition to words per minute and progress, Readwise—which is in an invite-only public beta mode but will be released to the wider public later this year—lets users see stats similar to those you might find in a sleep tracker. You can check if your reading has been “light,” or “active,” or “immersed.” (This feature is more experimental, Doyon said, and is based largely on how often people are highlighting phrases, looking up words, or taking notes.) I’m not sure, though, that tossing reading into the same good-for-you basket as eating your vegetables is a compelling pitch for an activity that already feels hard to many people. I expressed this reservation to Doyon, who reminded me that salad often actually tastes good. He said, “Working out feels good, right? It’s just hard to get into.” Doyon said that so far, Readwise seems to have two broad types of users. “There’s the group that’s in the self-improvement, quantified-self camp, and they like the data just because it’s got this aspect of self-discovery,” he said. The other group, he said, wants “keepsakes and mementos of activities they did. It’s kind of like taking a photo when you get to the top of a trail on a hike.” The data become a souvenir, something that can be shared with others. When I saw my stats for House of Mirth , though, I couldn’t make sense of them. Was 136 words per minute good, I wondered? I looked at the profiles of some of the other users, most of whom had higher WPM scores, many in the 200s. Well , I thought, isn’t Wharton’s prose more complicated than what you find in a contemporary self-help book? Wasn’t I reading slowly because I was savoring? And then: Why am I comparing myself at all? That can be one of the effects of tracking your activities—you suddenly find yourself in a race you’re not sure you signed up for. And reading is not running. I have run thousands of miles in my life—2,369.21 of which are recorded in my tracking app, the rest lost to history and shoddy data transfer. (Notice that even here, I’m subtly competing, telling you I’ve run more miles than the number captures.) The discipline involved in running is basically repetition: Get up; put your shoes on; get going; do it again. Of course, you run some memorable miles—hard ones, easy ones, fast ones, slow ones—but they are measurable and reducible to the same unit of distance. A mile is a mile, and your pace is the only thing that really changes. Over time, if all goes well, you get faster, or run farther, or both. [ Read: An underrated reason boys are reading less ] Reading is defined instead by how nonlinear it is. Each time you pick up a book, your human mind interacts with one specific piece of art, written (one hopes) by someone with another singular consciousness. Books cannot be equalized. Stats such as words per minute—what can they tell you, really, about the experience of reading something, other than that it was fast or slow? I’ve read some of the least-rewarding books of my life in less than a day. Others, I inhaled quickly because I loved them so much. I’ve read slowly because I’m enjoying a long journey, or because a book is a slog. Data flatten these experiences. That’s what statistics do, in reducing experiences to their component parts. items.title: Electric Lit’s Top 10 Poetry Collections of 2026
items.summary: This year’s most interesting poetry collections keep circling one small word: we . In an era when we’re constantly sorted into us and them , these poets ask who does the sorting and what it costs. Is we a people, a piece of land, a family, a crowd, a database? And where does that leave the rest of us, trying to keep up? Layli Long Soldier’s We (Wé) takes the question of we to its most elemental level. The Lakota word wé means blood, and Long Soldier uses it to explore family, nation, history, and language through poems, essays, and artwork. For Jake Skeets, we extends beyond people to the land and everything living on it. Horses opens with 200 feral horses stuck in Arizona mud and unfurls into an elegy for a changing Navajo Nation. Fatimah Asghar’s Daughter of the Mountains asks what remains after exile, reckoning with estranged kin and the landscape of their ancestors in poems both funny and elegiac. In Assembled Audience , the ever-delightful Erika Meitner takes up the strange business of being together, on beaches and in airports, in mourning and in protest. William Lessard’s haunting /face turns patents for facial capture technology into unlikely poetry about what happens when a face becomes data. And Hieu Minh Nguyen’s Staying Still traces the distance between the people and places we long to belong to and the selves we’re trying to become. So much about who counts as us is now decided by people and machines that don’t know us at all. Against all that flattening, these poems get stubbornly specific. Maybe we begins there, not in agreement or allegiance, but in the act of paying attention to what—and whom—we might otherwise overlook. –Kelly Luce Editor, The Commuter Editor’s note: The following books were hand-selected by Electric Literature staff and interns, with the help of our community of contributors, readers, and friends of the organization. While books by current staff or board members are not eligible for consideration, we would like to informally recommend I Can Tell You the Version That Will Make You Take My Side by board member J Brooke, another collection we loved this year! The 10 titles below are presented alphabetically by title; they are not ranked. /face by William Lessard If there’s something slightly absurd about composing an ode to the misty beauty of landscape on a Macbook Pro while pausing intermittently to check Instagram, take a selfie, take a screenshot, /face pinpoints it. William Lessard’s poetry accomplishes the seemingly impossible feat of writing in the tradition of powerpoints, patent filings, and the whole chaos of social media-fueled data harvesting that defines so much of life in 2026. Lessard’s book is not so much filled with traditionally formed poems as with shocks to the idea of what constitutes poetry; with experiments in embracing the parts of modern life that seem unfit for art; and, in short, with an unashamed attempt at authenticity. Read Lessard’s meditations on /face in an EL interview . . . and read the book! –Willem Marx , Associate Editor America, A Love Story by Camille T Dungy In America, A Love Story , Camille T Dungy addresses the nation with the exasperated, clear-eyed intimacy of someone who knows its capacity to wound. Writing as a Black woman and mother, Dungy turns love into an interrogation, pushing away the easy comfort of a flag-waving tribute. Her poems move fluidly from strawberry fields tarped against frost to a father questioned on a roadside, from a grandmother’s willow switch to the sleepless, fragile early days of parenting. Love, through these poems, is an enduring tenderness for daughters, for soil and blooming lilacs, for the hard-won instinct to protect what is vulnerable. In Dungy’s hands, love is what keeps imagination alive when safety falters, an unflinching devotion that refuses to ignore danger while still demanding that America answer back. – Shandela Contreras , Editorial Intern Assembled Audience by Erika Meitner In Assembled Audience , Erika Meitner looks straight at the conditions that make “staying present” feel like a moral demand: fracking, climate change, pandemic aftermath, gun violence, the erosion of reproductive rights. A peripatetic speaker moves from eschatology to a Hampton Inn, from Whitman-sized questions to Bud Light and dragonflies, making room for luck, wonder, and the strange comedy of being alive. Reading this collection, I was certainly reminded of the Whitmanesque impulse in “Song of Myself”—which is really the chorus of each other, the idea that to create and exist is to wonder, and that we celebrate our fractured world by relentlessly examining everything within it, finding interest even in the mundane. Meitner channels that expansive, defiant celebration into our own dizzying moment. In Meitner’s electric, unsentimental vision of all its gatherings, attention itself becomes a way of standing with others. – Shandela Contreras , Editorial Intern Daughters of the Mountains by Fatimah Asghar Unafraid of tackling the vastness of human experience from love to loss, Asghar asks how an exile can find their place in the world. What follows are meditative, at times humorous, and always introspective poems that embrace the complexities of lineage, environment, family, and nature in shaping and disrupting home and the self. If you’re a fan of poetry dealing with queerness, displacement, or searching for connection, there’s a lot to be said for Daughter of the Mountains. –Rachel Maybee , Editorial Intern Horses by Jake Skeets Beginning with the evocative image of 200 horses found dead in the mud of a former stock pond on Navajo land in Arizona, Navajo Nation Poet Laureate Jake Skeets faces down environmental apocalypse and dares to allow hope to blossom from grief. Queer, lyrical, and inextricable from Diné thought, Skeets’ poems span time and distance, blurring the artificial boundary set between people and place. This gorgeous, highly-anticipated second collection will leave readers marking Skeets as a poet to watch. –Rachel Maybee , Editorial Intern Maybe the Body by Asa Drake In his introduction to EL’s interview with Asa Drake , Cameron Quan describes reading her gorgeous debut collection as not unlike “the experience of being cared for at a distance.” I, editor of that interview, rushed to read Drake’s book myself. Quan is right, a sense of care emanates from Drake’s words. Yet what continues to resonate now, as the year comes to a close and Drake’s book still lingers in my mind, is the way it demonstrates how to care. These poems tease out the crystalline threads that connect a self and a body, a body and a world, a place and a history, and in doing so, demonstrate a stunning capacity to observe. To observe this carefully is to care radically. Drake writes: “When I feed the animals / the rabbit stands up // so straight she falls over. / This is the part I want / you to know.” Maybe the Body is the kind of book that is both splash and ripple, sound and echo. – Willem Marx , Associate Editor Run It Back by Kortney Morrow In Run it Back , Kortney Morrow’s debut poetry collection, nostalgia takes center stage. We float through a luminous remembrance of the early 2000s, a time when freedom felt inevitable and aspiration felt a mere breath away. Hope and heroics are the lifeblood of this collection, much like “the hero” (in this case, Lebron James) injects life into his community, uplifts the people, and they, in turn, become their own heroes. As a fellow Cleveland native, this collection was especially important to read; it is a tribute to the power of a place—and a people—that has long felt forgotten. Morrow reminds us, in this stunning and timely collection, that learning the past is the key to unlocking our future. –Denne Michele Norris , Executive Director and Publisher Staying Still by Hieu Minh Nguyen In Staying Still , Hieu Minh Nguyen treats remaining alive as an arduous, tender labor. items.title: In the Midst of Bingeing and Purging, My Job Theft Was A Silent Cry for Help
items.summary: Stealing Space by Dayna Mahannah The gas station’s fluorescent lights glowed as I waited for the vehicles to clear their pumps. When the lot had emptied, I abandoned the till. I roamed the aisles, straightening candy products and rearranging the Hungry Man sub sandwiches in the fridge. The security camera had a blind spot where I could wedge myself, right up against the counter. I snuck a Danish, the syrupy glaze clinging to the wrapper like mucus. I chewed fast, facing the wall, and stuffed the packaging in the coffee station trash. After pretending to organize the chocolate bar display in front of the till, I swiped a Mr. Big off the shelf, tucking it under the edge of my work shirt, and pushed open the side exit into the garage. Light beamed into the defunct repair shop. Dust motes glimmered, floating in the dark like phosphorescent plankton. Then the door shut, severing the shaft of light. Petroleum wafted up from the concrete floor. Standing on the stoop, my skin hot despite the frigid shop, I tore through the serrated edge of the candy wrapper, scarfing the chewy mess. I jammed the yellow wrapper underneath used oil containers in the recycling drum. We experimented with tiny crimes like egging houses and stealing makeup from Zellers. Back inside the station, a cursory check out the window showed no customers gassing up. I flipped the Back in 5 Minutes sign on the front door, turned the lock, raced for the bathroom, and drove my fingers down my esophagus until everything pushed out into the open. I’d started working at the gas station in June, just as grade 10 was petering off and the warmer Okanagan days were stretching out like a promise. That first year of high school my friends and I cemented ourselves together with secrets and sleepovers and the second-last season of The O.C . We broke loose in the summer, splintered into new alliances, graduated from gossiping about crushes to hooking up in the dark at bush parties. We experimented with tiny crimes like egging houses and stealing makeup from Zellers. I pulled my first all-nighter and showed up to my Saturday shift at the station, appalled at how great I felt. Hangovers didn’t catch up to 16-year-olds. My boss, Kevin, owned the gas station, which stood on a busy corner in Westbank (now West Kelowna) where the old highway intersected the new highway that funneled people out of town. Kevin, curly-haired and stocky, must have been in his 30s—maybe even the same age I am now, 36. Really nice guy. Organized. Good-natured and even-keeled but took his business seriously. Always looked like he’d just polished off a great cup of coffee. Kevin trained me behind the till. He taught me to make eye contact with every customer who drove into the lot. This helped prevent fill ‘n’ runs, since in 2006 you filled first, paid second. He told me that people were less likely to act on a bad intention when they felt acknowledged. When a customer forgot their points card, we were to instruct them to bring the receipt on their next visit. Kevin showed me how to manually add points to a customer’s card by typing in the dollar total, scanning the points card, then deleting the amount from the computer. Using the clunky Knuckle Buster, we’d imprint the points card on carbon paper. Initial the customer’s receipt so they couldn’t double back for points. People didn’t forget their cards often, but they forgot them regularly. The points system worked like most: spend money, rack up points, redeem for goods—slurpees, propane, firewood, fuel. On the counter next to the rack of wraparound sunglasses stood a turnstile bejewelled with shiny plastic gift cards glued to cardboard backings, their denominations printed in white in the top corner. Each rotation revealed a higher number. $25. $50. $100. “How long does it take to save up for something like that?” I had asked when Kevin explained that points could even be redeemed for gift cards. A long time, was all he said. To me, that meant years . A unit of time that adults measured life by. My social studies teacher talked about the world in years and it seemed so irrelevant that I skipped that class the most. I could see only as far ahead as the end of the next work schedule. When grade 11 started that fall, I switched to evening and weekend shifts and often worked alone for hours at a time. I would show up for my shift at 4:00 PM. At 5:00 PM, my coworker Janice pulled a sweater over her uniform, lighter and cigarette in hand as she waved goodbye. The shift commenced in sales: Coke slushies and tanks of diesel to long-haul truckers, Lotto Max tickets and regular fuel to moms in Von Dutch trucker hats and frosted lip gloss. But there was the space between sales, too. All that alone time. Crispy Crunch. Old Dutch BBQ chips. At a low point, I gobbled one of the Hungry Mans, a sandwich more self-assured than I dreamed of being. Grade 10 had been an excellent year for my eating disorder. I’d been so vigilant, eating privately within a restricted time frame, followed by an immediate purge. I became skinny enough that people started asking if I was okay. The goal was not to take up less space, but to accumulate space—between my thighs, between my stomach and waistband. Indiscriminate, space started to wedge itself between everything: me and other people, me and myself. The space was my secret. And all I wanted was more and more space. Now, in grade 11, I was getting sloppy. I ate in less controlled environments: here at work, surrounded by food, where variables such as cleaning duties and paying customers disrupted the conditions necessary for my carefully orchestrated process. Over the winter, my body revolted. Chided by sandwich displays and endless rows of bright packaging, it sneaked and snatched and stuffed and swallowed. Then I’d ring in Paydays and Gold Rush tickets and cartons of Export A Gold, smiling at customers through the silent horror of the digestive process occurring in my body, the calories accumulating, absorbing, storing. I’d lost control—every chip and Danish transmuting into extra flesh. Bubbling over the waistband of my Lululemon tights. The spaces that I coveted shrank. People stopped asking if I was okay. Still, my secret flourished. Snow melted on sidewalks the day I took an imprint of a customer’s points card and entered the dollar amount into the computer. I did it twice—once to load the points onto their card. A second time, after they left, to load the same amount onto my own. I recall thinking that a double charge of the same figure could be called a mistake if it showed on the records. Which it wouldn’t—no imprint, no record. Only when a customer redeemed points did their card show up in the system. Since I wasn’t totally reckless, I didn’t swipe points again for a long time. Instead, I ate. And I hid. And I hid and I ate. I felt just as nervous about the prospect of being caught sneaking points as I did being caught with my mouth muddied with chocolate. But the former transgression only made me feel guilty. The latter? Shame. My hunger had greater control over me than I had over it. Swiping the points, however, felt deliberate, calculated. No sloppiness here. Another secret, but a case over which I held jurisdiction. After a couple weeks, Kevin had still made no mention of the unaccounted-for points. He greeted me the same as usual each shift. A warm smile. Eye contact. Occasionally, a dad joke. When Kevin headed for the garage where he parked his car, I looked him in the eye and wished him a good night. I began to match points on my own card every time a customer handed me their receipt from a day they had forgotten theirs. Twenty or, if I was lucky, 50 bucks a pop. But they didn’t forget often enough. The gift cards hung next to the till on their cardboard backings. Free money. Awaiting activation. items.title: NASA’s next flagship to answer the biggest question: “Are we alone?”
items.summary: There are a few questions that humanity has always pondered, yet scarcely could satisfactorily answer until the proper scientific advances came along. Questions like: What is the Universe? Where did it come from? How did it get to be this way? And what is its ultimate fate? are questions that have been with us since time immemorial, yet remained unanswerable for nearly all of human history. Beginning in the 20th century and now into the 21st century, many of these questions are finally getting comprehensive answers thanks to incredible advances in physics and astronomy. However, perhaps the biggest question of all — the question of “Are we alone in the Universe?” — remains as perhaps the greatest existential unanswered question of all. While the current generation of ground-based and space-based telescopes can take us far into the Universe, this is a question that’s currently the reach of any observatory that presently exists. To get there, we’ll need to acquire direct images of Earth-like exoplanets: planets with sizes and temperatures similar to Earth, but that orbit Sun-like stars, not the more common red dwarf stars like Proxima Centauri or TRAPPIST-1. Those capabilities are precisely what NASA is aiming for with its next flagship mission: the Habitable Worlds Observatory . It’s an ambitious project, sure, but one that’s well worth it. After all, finding out we’re not alone in the Universe would quite possibly be the biggest revolution in all of science history. This animation shows the four super-Jupiter planets directly imaged in orbit around the star HR 8799, whose light is blocked by a coronagraph. The four exoplanets shown here are among the easiest to directly image owing to their large size and brightness, as well as their huge separation from their parent star. Our ability to directly image exoplanets is constrained to giant exoplanets at great distances from bright stars, but improvements in coronagraph technology will dramatically change that story. Credit : Jason Wang (Northwestern)/William Thompson (UVic)/Christian Marois (NRC Herzberg)/Quinn Konopacky (UCSD) At the present time, there are three main ways we’re actively searching for alien life . We’re exploring worlds in our Solar System, including Mars, Venus, Titan, Europa, and Pluto, remotely and in situ , with fly-by missions, orbiters, landers, and even rovers, searching for evidence of past life or even, potentially simple life that persists at the present time. We’re examining exoplanets, searching for evidence that there’s life on them, from the surface to the atmosphere and beyond, based on observable signatures of color, seasonal change, and atmospheric contents. And by looking for any signals that would reveal the presence of intelligent aliens: through efforts such as SETI and Breakthrough Listen. All three approaches have their advantages and disadvantages , and so it makes sense to invest in all three. As long as we don’t find anyone else, we’ll have no choice but to wonder whether we’re alone or not . However, once we have a successful example of life that originated outside of Earth, we’ll know for certain that we have company here in the cosmos. Given the sheer number of chances that are out there, most scientists believe that it’s the second option that’s most likely to deliver our first success. If life requires conditions similar to those found on Earth, we might well be the only world in the Solar System where life ever developed, survived, thrived, became technologically advanced, and still exists at the present time. Unless there are other intelligent, actively broadcasting civilizations nearby right now, endeavors like SETI won’t be able deliver any positive results. However, “life of any type” is a much lower bar than actively-transmitting intelligent, technologically advanced civilizations. If even a small fraction of worlds that exist with Earth-like properties have life of any type on them, exoplanet studies can deliver a success where the other two options won’t. And we’ve come a very long way in our studies of exoplanets: we have more than 6000 known, confirmed exoplanets within the Milky Way, where we know the mass, radius, and orbital period of nearly all of those confirmed worlds. Although more than 6,000 confirmed exoplanets are now known, with more than half of them uncovered by Kepler, there are no true analogues of the planets found in our Solar System. Jupiter-analogues, Earth-analogues, and Mercury-analogues all remain elusive with current technology. The overwhelming majority of planets found via the transit method are close to their parent star, are ~10% the radius (or, equivalently, ~1% the surface area) of their parent star or more, and are orbiting low-mass, small-sized stars. Credit : NASA/Ames/Jessie Dotson and Wendy Stenzel; annotated by E. Siegel Unfortunately, this isn’t enough to inform us about whether any of these worlds are inhabited. To make that determination, we need more than that. We’d need to be able to make the necessary measurements that could answer such questions as: Does the exoplanet have an atmosphere? Does it have clouds, precipitation, and weather cycles? Do its continents green-and-brown with the seasons, like they do on Earth? Does it have gases or gas combinations in its atmosphere that hint at biological activity, and do they show seasonal variations like Earth’s CO2 levels do? On the cutting edge of performing these measurements, today, are the space-based JWST and ground-based 10-meter class telescopes, performing direct exoplanet imaging and transit spectroscopy. But even those great observatories are not enough to reach the goal we’re truly after. JWST and 10-meter ground-based telescopes cannot measure the properties of Earth-sized planets in Earth-like orbits around Sun-like stars. For direct imaging studies, we can take pictures of planets that are the size of Jupiter and that are more than about Saturn’s distance from the Sun: good for gas giant worlds, but not so great for looking for life on rocky planets. For transit spectroscopy, we can see the light that filters through the atmospheres of super-Earth-sized worlds around red dwarf stars, but Earth-sized planets around Sun-like stars are well beyond the reach of current technology. When starlight passes through a transiting exoplanet’s atmosphere, signatures are imprinted. Depending on the wavelength and intensity of both emission and absorption features, the presence or absence of various atomic and molecular species within an exoplanet’s atmosphere can be revealed through the technique of transit spectroscopy. JWST cannot get spectra for Earth-sized planets around Sun-like stars, but Habitable Worlds Observatory finally will. Credit : ESA/David Sing/PLAnetary Transits and Oscillations of stars (PLATO) mission We have, however, come far enough to know that if we can scale up our technology, acquiring that data for the exoplanets we truly desire is possible. What we need to do is build on our current technology and enhance it further if we hope to find and characterize an actually inhabited planet. Currently, we’re building the next generation of ground-based telescopes, ushering in the era of 30-meter class telescopes with the GMTO , the ELT , and potentially Exo-Life Finder as well , and looking forward to the exquisite performance of the coronagraph aboard NASA’s next astrophysics flagship mission: the Nancy Roman Telescope. The Roman telescope will have the same capabilities as Hubble but with superior instrumentation, a field-of-view that’s 50-100 times as great as Hubble’s, and a coronagraph that allows us to image planets within the glare of their parent star’s light that are about 1000 times fainter than JWST can see.
